profile: Michael Inman of Harrodsburg entered the Associated Students Congress by the class-officer route, elected sophomore class vice-president in the spring of 1972 alongside president Louis Berman. The 1973 Talisman recorded that the sophomores were the second largest class on the Hill but were not active in many class projects, their one major undertaking being to sponsor Elaine Leftwich as a Homecoming queen candidate.

Terry Miller reached the Associated Students Congress through two consecutive class offices. The 1972 Talisman recorded him as junior class vice-president for 1971-72, in a slate of five class officers headed by president Ed Jordan, who became Associated Students president the following year. For 1972-73 Miller was elected senior class president, with Joe Cheak as vice-president.

The 1973 Talisman recorded that the number of class officers had been cut to two that year, and that Miller and Cheak understood their responsibility as representing the class in the Associated Students Congress; the yearbook reported that class activity was otherwise nil, the only class project being to sponsor Lee Davis as a Homecoming queen candidate.

Fred Price.seat: Congress member; junior class president; co-head, Rules and Elections Committee
profile: Fred Price was elected junior class president for 1972-73 with Gail Emberton as vice-president. The 1973 Talisman noted that under the revised Associated Students constitution only the top two class officers were retained, and that class presidents and vice-presidents had previously been allowed to vote in Congress. The yearbook recorded the class's Homecoming float as winner of the Red Towel Award, with Debby Clark as its queen candidate.

The same yearbook recorded the Rules and Elections Committee, which handles campus elections and hears election disputes, as headed by R. G. Meade and Fred Price. That committee was tested in the first week of November 1972, when a voting discrepancy forced a special election for Homecoming queen; the Herald of 4 November 1972 carried the story alongside an item headlined that Fred Price said the committee would investigate the election.

Price stood for Associated Student Government administrative vice president in the spring of 1973. The Herald of 6 April 1973 printed the platforms of the two hopefuls for the office, Glenn Jackson and Fred Price. Jackson took the post for 1973-74. Price was a member of the Pi Kappa Phi colony, which received its national charter during his time at Western.

Gail Emberton was elected junior class vice-president for 1972-73, serving under president Fred Price. The 1973 Talisman recorded that the revised Associated Students constitution had cut the class slate to two officers, and that the class's Homecoming float, entered with Debby Clark as its queen candidate, won the Red Towel Award. The class also planned a dinner for its active members.

The 1974 Talisman named her to Who's Who among students, listing her as personnel chairman of Chi Omega, 1972-73 junior class vice-president, first runner-up in the Miss Three Alarm contest, and a President's Scholar.

A Gail Emberton bylined a sustained run of Herald housing and academic-affairs reporting across the same period, from dormitory occupancy in January 1973 through the Housing Committee's survey and its proposed policy revisions that spring. The archive has not confirmed from any source that the reporter and the class vice-president are the same person, and records the byline here without asserting it.

Ronda Talley.seat: Congress member; representative of the College of Education
profile: Ronda Talley sat in the Associated Students Congress in 1972-73 as the student representative from the College of Education. The 1973 Talisman recorded that she had been voted a representative to the Congress and named to the 1972 edition of Who's Who in American Colleges and Universities, one of two Kappa Delta members tapped that year.

The same yearbook recorded her other campus work: membership of Kappa Delta, the Student National Education Association and Lambda Chi Alpha's Crescent Club, which named her its 1972 Outstanding Crescent Girl. She was also a student contributor to the 1973 Talisman. Her account of her field described pre-schoolers as needing a skilled teacher to let them learn by personal discovery.

The yearbook's own pages spell the name two ways: Ronda in the Kappa Delta and Who's Who sections and in the name index, Rhonda in the Crescent Club caption and the Talisman staff list. The archive keeps the spelling its source used and flags the difference rather than settling it.

Carl Stoltzfus, an elementary education major from Cochranville, Pennsylvania, was recorded by the 1973 Talisman as a member of the Associated Students Government, the student member of the Academic Council from the College of Education, and a member of both the College of Education Curriculum Committee and the University Academic Complaint Committee. He and fellow Sigma Phi Epsilon member Mike Brandenberg represented their fraternity at the National Leadership Methods Convention.

He stood in the Associated Student Government election of spring 1973: the Herald of 13 April 1973, the issue that carried the election returns and a report on the installation of officers at the Congress party, printed a letter from him thanking his supporters. The archive has not established which office he sought.

For 1973-74 he was elected senior class president, with Hamp Moore as vice-president; the 1974 Talisman recorded the pair supervising the class's Homecoming activities and its Gone with the Wind float. That yearbook also listed him as chairman of the Associated Student Government's Rules and Elections Committee, public relations chairman of the Student National Education Association, Talisman Greek editor and a member of Who's Who.

The archive holds his surname in two spellings. The 1972-73 Congress record follows the source that gives Stolzfus; the Talisman name index, the fraternity pages and his own 4 December 1973 Herald letter give Stoltzfus. The difference is flagged, not resolved.

Melody Edwards, an agriculture major, was recorded by the 1974 Talisman as a representative in the Associated Student Government and on the Academic Council, and was named to Who's Who. Asked about involvement, she said getting involved was a good outlet as long as it stayed moderate.

Her other recorded campus work was in her field: she belonged to the Agriculture Club, whose Halloween carnival in 1972 the yearbook credited her with supplying its Great Pumpkin, and to the Agricultural Education Club. Of agriculture she said it was a field changing rapidly that needed people of both sexes willing to keep up.

Michael Inman moved up from sophomore class vice-president to junior class president for 1973-74, with Deborah Locke as vice-president. The 1974 Talisman recorded the pair coordinating the class's activities, which included a Fiddler on the Roof float in the Homecoming parade and a spring dance. He was also a junior ROTC student, photographed by the yearbook directing traffic as students converged on campus at the start of the year.

In April 1974 he was a public participant in the contest for the student seat on the Board of Regents. The Herald of 19 April 1974, whose lead story reported that five students had filed for the seat, printed a letter under his name headlined "Inman Announces"; the same issue carried an endorsement letter for another candidate, Hamp Moore. The 25 April vote produced no winner outright, and the Herald of 26 April reported Greg McKinney and Sid Stevens contesting the run-off, which McKinney won.

Deborah Locke was elected junior class vice-president for 1973-74, serving with president Michael Inman; the 1974 Talisman recorded the two coordinating the class's Homecoming float and a planned spring dance, and named her among the Kappa Delta members who had distinguished themselves on campus. The 1975 Talisman's name index lists her as Deborah J. Locke Brooks, the yearbook's own record of a changed surname.

Hamp Moore was elected senior class vice-president for 1973-74 under president Carl Stoltzfus. The 1974 Talisman recorded the two supervising the class's Homecoming activities, including its Gone with the Wind float, and listed Moore among the seniors receiving outside honours that year as vice-president of the Southeast Regional Inter-Fraternity Conference. He was a member of Sigma Alpha Epsilon and appears in the yearbook at that fraternity's signing of its scroll before the run to Middle Tennessee, alongside university president Dero Downing.

He stood in the April 1974 election for the student seat on the Board of Regents. The Herald printed endorsement letters for him in both issues covering the race, from Bruce Merrick on 19 April, the issue whose lead reported that five students had filed, and from Gail Getchell on 23 April, the issue in which the candidates listed their qualifications. He did not reach the run-off, which the Herald of 26 April reported as a contest between Greg McKinney and Sid Stevens.

Debbie Filburn sat in the Associated Student Government Congress as a representative-at-large in 1973-74; the 1974 Talisman named her among the Kappa Delta members who had distinguished themselves on campus, in that office. She had been a student contributor to the 1973 Talisman the year before.

The 1975 Talisman recorded that two sisters, Donna and Debbie Filburn, were both in the Associated Student Government. They are two people, and the archive records them separately: Donna Filburn sat in the 1974-75 Congress and was Panhellenic Council president.

John Donofrio, Jr. was elected freshman class president for 1973-74, with Christy Kay Vogt as vice-president. The 1974 Talisman headed its account of the class "Donofrio and Vogt lead freshman class" and recorded their first major project as a Homecoming float on the theme of Camelot, with Marcia Heckman as the class's queen candidate and a concert-dance planned for the spring. The pair were photographed in the Helm library.
His vice-president that year went on to be administrative vice president of the Associated Student Government in 1975-76 and its president in 1976-77, under the name Christy Vogt.

Jeff Wampler, a pre-med major from Jeffersontown, was elected sophomore class vice-president for 1973-74, serving under president Steve Henry. The 1974 Talisman recorded that seven sophomores sat in the Associated Student Government Congress that year, and photographed the two class officers checking notes before an Associated Student Government meeting; the class's executive committee had tentatively planned a free dance for the spring.
He was a member of Sigma Alpha Epsilon, and the Herald of 18 October 1974 printed a letter from him thanking the workers on the fraternity's Homecoming float.

Mike Inman completed three consecutive years in the Associated Student Government Congress by way of class office, elected senior class president for 1974-75 with Pam Stewart as vice-president. The 1975 Talisman recorded that only the two of them attended the meeting called to organise the class's Homecoming contribution, for a class of 1,865, and that they rented the Harrodsburg Heritage mobile history unit rather than build a float.

The yearbook printed his own account of why he sought class office: he said he ran for it because it was the easiest way of getting a seat on the student government. He held that the office itself was of little consequence, since by their senior year students had little class unity, and proposed a bill to abolish class officers and replace them with congress representatives elected from each class. Student government president Jeff Consolo opposed the bill. Inman argued that class officers carried a little more prestige than representatives-at-large but that there should be no distinction among members.

He was elected to Who's Who and was president of the Omicron Delta Kappa National Leadership Society. He was a member of the Scabbard and Blade military honour corps and was second runner-up for the national Mayer-Raeburn Scholarship Award. Asked to name his chief accomplishment from a list that included the presidencies of his junior and senior classes and the vice-presidency of his sophomore class, he chose his involvement in ROTC, and said the most important part of his college education had come from his participation in campus activities rather than from the classroom.

Jeff Wampler was elected junior class president for 1974-75, moving up from the sophomore class vice-presidency, with Karen McNally as his vice-president. The 1975 Talisman recorded that their main function as officers was to attend meetings of the Associated Student Government.

The same account recorded both officers saying there was really no need for class officers, even though they had worked hard to get elected. McNally said students had no interest in class activities, that they called class meetings and nobody came, and that what was needed instead was more representatives-at-large in the Associated Student Government. The judgement matched that of the senior class president the same year, Mike Inman, who put a bill to abolish class officers altogether.

He was elected to Who's Who, one of four Sigma Alpha Epsilon members named in the 1976 Talisman. Asked by that yearbook what Western needed, he said students and the administration must both learn to bend towards the middle, and that until that communication was accomplished students would remain apathetic toward student elections and concerts.
